newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: United Nations ends sanctions against Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: United Nations ends sanctions against Belgrade.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Tuesday formally ended trade sanctions against the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro imposed in 1992 for their role in fomenting the war in Bosnia.
Sanctions against Yugoslavia as well as Bosnian Serbs were suspended by the council last November as a followup to their participation in the U.S.-initiated Dayton peace accords.
The council at that time stipulated the sanctions -- a stringent trade embargo and a travel and transport ban -- would be lifted entirely after this year's Bosnian elections, held on September 14.
"It is positive both for us and the international community which by this act fulfilled its own commitment with the Dayton peace process," said Yugoslavia's U.N. envoy Vladislav Jovanovic.

The resolution, approved by a 15-0 vote, "terminates with immediate effect" the May 1992 sanctions. The Honduran foreign minister, Delmer Urbizo Panting, chaired the meeting on the first day of his country's presidency of the council.

The document warned, however, that the council would consider reimposing any of the sanctions if Yugoslavia or the Serbs failed "significantly to meet its obligations under the (Dayton) peace agreement." But most diplomats considered it unlikely Russia would vote to restore any of the embargoes.

To the disappointment of Russia, the resolution, at the insistence of the United States, did not end the suspension of Yugoslavia from the U.N. General Assembly and other U.N. bodies mainly because of its disputed legal status.
It also did not release Belgrade's frozen assets because of disputes and claims from successor states, such as Croatia, Bosnia, Slovenia and Macedonia, after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia.

Russia's U.N. ambassador, Sergei Lavrov, said he had wanted the resolution to cover Belgrade's re-admission to U.N. bodies "but others put more linkages" into the issue than the General Assembly, itself had done.
"Their only condition was that the war should stop and the war has stopped long ago," he told reporters.
But he aid that lifting the sanctions should help Belgrade conduct its trade "on a firmer basis and stimpulate exchanges."

In addition, the United States and Europeans will keep in place a so-called outer ring of sanctions, such as preventing the rump Yugoslav state of Serbia and Montenegro from institutions like the International Monetary Fund.

Britain's Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind said last week that Western European states have linked Yugoslavia's re-entry to financial institutions to progress on the restive Serbian province of Kosovo, dominated by ethnic Albanians.
Washington this week agreed to the resolution after the September 14 Bosnian elections were certified on Sunday by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
